paper_title: SplatAnything: Gaussian Spacing Normalization for Feed-forward 3DGS across Arbitrary Scenes

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We identify a key limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods: Gaussian attributes are typically predicted in a radial-distance-normalized space that canonicalizes a global radial statistic of the reconstructed geometry, while the spacing between neighboring Gaussian centers can still vary substantially across scene scales and camera configurations. This mismatch induces systematic shifts in Gaussian-scale targets, leading to ambiguous supervision. To address this, we propose SplatAnything with Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm), which canonicalizes a robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing to provide a more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction. To rigorously assess our method, we further establish a systematic benchmark spanning diverse datasets, input sparsity levels, and challenging extrapolated viewpoints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SplatAnything achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong gains under substantial variations in scene scale and viewpoint.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) directly predicts 3D Gaussian representation (Kerbl et al., 2023) from input images, avoiding the costly per-scene optimization of conventional 3DGS. This efficiency makes it attractive for large-scale 3D reconstruction and digital content creation. The ultimate goal is single model that generalizes reliably across arbitrary scene scales, camera configurations, and target viewpoints, yet such broad generalization remains challenging. prevailing paradigm is to first predict per-pixel depth using geometry foundation model (Wang et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026), and then predict per-pixel Gaussian attributes based on the resulting geometry in its radial-distance-normalized coordinate space. Radial Distance Normalization (RDNorm) uses the mean radial distance of reconstructed 3D points to the reference-camera origin as scene-level scale, and globally rescales the scene to canonicalize this statistic. However, RDNorm does not directly canonicalize the spacing between neighboring Gaussian centers, which we refer to as Gaussian spacing. Since adequate surface coverage requires the Gaussian scale to match the local Gaussian spacing, variations in this quantity directly induce shifts in the corresponding learning targets. As illustrated in Fig. 2, visually similar regions can exhibit substantially different Gaussian spacings after RDNorm under different scene scales and camera configurations. Consequently, similar local observations may correspond to different Gaussian-scale targets across scenes, introducing ambiguity in scale supervision. predictor biased toward smaller Gaussian scales may under-cover regions with large Gaussian spacing and produce holes, whereas one biased toward larger scales may cause excessive overlap in densely sampled regions and lead to over-smoothing, as shown in Fig. 7. This ambiguity in Gaussian-scale supervision poses major bottleneck to robust feed-forward 3DGS generalization across varying scene scales and camera configurations. To address this issue, we introduce SplatAnything, feed-forward 3DGS framework equipped with Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm). The key idea of GSNorm is to derive the scene-level normalization factor from representative statistic of Gaussian spacing, rather than from global radial statistic. Under the per-pixel Gaussian prediction paradigm, where each valid image pixel corresponds to Gaussian center, perspective projection relates Gaussian spacing to scene depth and camera intrinsics. Based on this relation, GSNorm computes Gaussian spacing over all valid observations and uses its median as robust scene-level normalization factor. The reconstructed geometry is then rescaled accordingly, canonicalizing the representative Gaussian spacing across scenes. This provides more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian-scale prediction, alleviating ambiguity in supervision caused by variations in scene scale and camera configuration and thereby improving generalization across diverse scenes and viewpoints. To rigorously assess SplatAnything and prior methods, we further introduce cross-dataset benchmark for in-the-wild evaluation. Unlike conventional protocols (Wang et al., 2026a; Xu et al., 2025b;a; Ye et al., 2026; Ren et al., 2026), which often focus on training-related domains and interpolated target views, our benchmark covers diverse datasets, scene scales, image resolutions, and camera configurations, while explicitly varying input-view sparsity and emphasizing challenging Figure 2: Normalization space. (a) Radial Distance Normalization canonicalizes global radial statistic but leaves Gaussian spacing varying across scenes and camera configurations, resulting in inconsistent supervision targets. (b) Gaussian Spacing Normalization canonicalizes representative statistic of Gaussian spacing, providing more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction. extrapolated viewpoints. Extensive experiments show that SplatAnything achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong gains under large scene and viewpoint shifts. In summary, our contributions are: We identify ambiguity in Gaussian-scale supervision across varying scene scales and camera configurations induced by RDNorm. To address this issue, we propose Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm), which canonicalizes robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing to provide more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction. We establish systematic cross-dataset evaluation benchmark for feed-forward 3DGS, spanning diverse scene categories, image resolutions, camera configurations, input-view sparsity levels, and challenging extrapolated viewpoints. This benchmark enables controlled evaluation of cross-scene and cross-view generalization.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Geometry foundation models. Recent feed-forward geometry foundation models (Wang et al., 2024; 2025; Lin et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2026) directly recover depth, point maps, and camera poses from RGB observations, providing strong geometric priors across diverse scenes. These models typically employ radial distance normalization to keep reconstructed geometry within numerically stable range. While effective for geometry prediction, such normalization does not ensure consistent Gaussian spacing across scenes, cameras, and image resolutions. This becomes critical when the normalized geometry is reused for per-pixel Gaussian prediction, since Gaussian scales are defined in the same 3D coordinate system. Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting. Feed-forward 3DGS methods directly infer Gaussian representations from image observations, often by first estimating per-pixel depth and then predicting Gaussian attributes. pixelSplat (Charatan et al., 2024) reconstructs 3D Gaussians from image pairs by learning 3D probability distribution over Gaussian centers. DepthSplat (Xu et al., 2025b) combines monocular depth priors with multi-view matching, while ReSplat (Xu et al., 2025a) further refines predicted Gaussians through rendering-based optimization. However, limited geometric accuracy can become bottleneck under large viewpoint extrapolation. More recent methods (Jiang et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026; Anonymous, 2027) leverage strong geometry foundation models to initialize Gaussian centers and predict the remaining attributes. Although this substantially improves reconstruction quality, these methods still inherit the radial-distance-normalized space of their geometry backbones, in which Gaussian spacing can vary substantially across scene scales and camera configurations, leading to ambiguity in Gaussian-scale supervision. Such supervision ambiguity makes it difficult to learn single Gaussian predictor that generalizes reliably across diverse input settings. Other approaches (An et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026) do not rely on explicit geometric priors. While they can achieve strong rendering quality at interpolated viewpoints, the learned Gaussian geometry can become less reliable under large viewpoint extrapolation.

sections.content: Existing benchmarks are typically concentrated on small set of datasets and evaluate interpolated target views, making it difficult to assess cross-domain and viewpoint generalization. To provide more comprehensive evaluation, we design new benchmark with the following properties: Cross-domain and cross-scale coverage. We evaluate on seven datasets: ScanNet (Dai et al., 2017), NRGBD (Azinovic et al., 2022), DL3DV (Ling et al., 2024), Tanks and Temples (Knapitsch et al., 2017), Mip-NeRF 360 (Barron et al., 2022), ETH3D (Schops et al., 2017), and DTU (Jensen et al., 2014). These datasets span wide range of physical scene scales, providing substantially broader test of cross-domain and cross-scale generalization. Controlled extrapolation and observation sparsity. We sample context views from compact trajectory span and select target views using an occlusion-aware symmetric co-visibility criterion. The inputtarget overlap is controlled within 0.20.6, with lower overlap corresponding to more challenging extrapolation. sections.title: 4.5 ABLATION STUDIES
sections.content: Effect of Gaussian spacing normalization. We ablate the normalization space for Gaussian prediction in Table 3, comparing RDNorm, RDNorm with scale calibration, and GSNorm under the same architecture and training settings. For RDNorm with scale calibration, Gaussian prediction remains in the RDNorm space, while the predicted Gaussian scales are uniformly rescaled to match the scenes median Gaussian spacing. Both RDNorm variants remain consistently inferior to GSNorm. Qualitatively, RDNorm tends to produce holes in small object-centric scenes and over-smoothed results in large outdoor scenes  (Fig. 7)  . Scale calibration alleviates the holes on object-centric scenes, but often turns them into over-smoothed reconstructions, while outdoor scenes remain blurry. These results indicate that post-prediction scale correction cannot resolve the ambiguity in scale supervision introduced by RDNorm. By canonicalizing the representative Gaussian spacing scale before Gaussian prediction, GSNorm provides better-aligned prediction space and yields more complete and sharper reconstructions across diverse scenes. Additional results are provided in the appendix. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We identified key limitation of existing methods: Radial Distance Normalization (RDNorm) does not directly normalize Gaussian spacing, leading to ambiguity in Gaussian-scale supervision across scene scales and camera configurations. To address this issue, we introduced SplatAnything with Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm), which derives scene-level normalization factor from representative statistic of Gaussian spacing and provides more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction. We further established systematic cross-dataset benchmark covering different input sparsity levels and challenging extrapolated viewpoints. Experiments demonstrate that SplatAnything achieves the strongest performance across most evaluation settings, highlighting the effectiveness of GSNorm and marking substantial step toward feed-forward 3DGS. Limitations and Future Work. SplatAnything relies on geometric priors from geometry foundation model and may degrade when reliable geometry cannot be recovered from extremely sparse or challenging inputs. It also primarily reconstructs regions visible in the input views, which can leave holes in unobserved areas. Future work will explore more robust geometry estimation and generative priors for completing unobserved regions.

We design multiple strategies to construct the training pairs for SplatAnything. Source-View Sampling Strategy. We construct source views to cover diverse camera-motion patterns while maintaining sufficient geometric overlap for reliable reconstruction by the geometry foundation model. We consider four representative trajectory patterns: forward-traversal, where the camera moves primarily along the viewing direction; lateral-sweep, where the camera translates mainly sideways while maintaining similar viewing direction; outward-looking, where the camera remains approximately stationary and rotates to observe different directions; and inward-orbit, where the camera moves around local region while maintaining an inward-facing view toward that region. For trajectories with substantial translation, we further vary the sampling stride to produce either densely overlapping or wide-baseline source views, covering different levels of parallax and input sparsity. During training, the trajectory pattern and sampling stride are randomly selected from dataset-specific mixture, with distance and stride budgets adapted to each dataset. Validation uses fixed deterministic sampling configuration for reproducibility. Examples of the different source-view sampling patterns are shown in Fig. 8. Sampling strategy for target views. Our target-view sampling aims to provide supervision across diverse viewpoint changes, ranging from interpolation to challenging extrapolation, in order to improve the viewpoint generalization ability of our model. For interpolation views, we select held-out view between the input views; for extrapolation views, we randomly sample diverse extrapolation patterns, including advancing along the camera trajectory to inspect local scene details at closer range, as well as moving away from the observed trajectory to view the scene from novel positions and orientations. The visualization of different target-view sampling modes are shown in Fig. 9. A.3 EVALUATION BENCHMARK DETAILS We provide additional details of the evaluation benchmark introduced in the main paper. Our benchmark spans seven datasets and evaluates different input-view counts of 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64. The protocol is designed to independently control input-view sparsity and target-view difficulty, while ensuring identical evaluation conditions across methods. 14 Figure 8: Source-view trajectory patterns (16 views per panel), visualized in an approximately top-down projection. Dots and arrows denote camera centers and viewing directions, respectively; the gray polyline connects consecutive views, and color indicates capture order. For inward-orbit, marks the approximate viewing center. Figure 9: Target-view sampling modes used during training. Blue cameras denote the source views provided as input, while red cameras denote the target views used for rendering supervision. Source-view construction. Instead of distributing the source views uniformly over the entire capture, we sample them from compact contiguous arc of the camera trajectory. This design leaves meaningful portion of the capture outside the observed region, making it possible to evaluate genuinely extrapolated novel views rather than views that are always bracketed by the inputs. To make different input-view counts directly comparable, we adopt fixed-span strategy. For each scene, we first determine the trajectory span at the sparsest setting of 4 source views. We select the widest arc whose adjacent source-view pairs maintain sufficient geometric overlap, measured by symmetric co-visibility; specifically, the 20-th percentile of adjacent-pair co-visibility is required to be at least 0.35. The resulting span and offset are then reused for 8, 16, 32, and 64 views, with additional views inserted within the same trajectory range. Therefore, all view-count settings share the same spatial coverage, and only the observation density changes. This allows the effect of input sparsity to be evaluated without conflating it with changes in scene coverage. Target-view selection. Target views are sampled from frames outside the source-view arc and are selected according to an occlusion-aware symmetric co-visibility measure. For each candidate target view, valid pixels are back-projected using ground-truth depth and projected into the source views. Pixels that are geometrically consistent with at least one source view are treated as observed, while occluded and out-of-frustum pixels reduce the overlap score; pixels for which visibility cannot be determined due to invalid depth are excluded from the statistic. We compute co-visibility in both projection directions and define Csym = min (Cfwd, Cbwd) . (15) 15 The symmetric formulation is important for asymmetric camera motions, such as moving toward the scene, where one-sided overlap measure can remain high even under substantial viewpoint change. We evaluate up to 40 candidate target views per scene and retain those whose symmetric co-visibility lies in 0.20 Csym < 0.60. (16) Up to four target views are selected from this interval, prioritizing lower co-visibility and, when necessary, larger parallax. In this way, target-view difficulty is explicitly controlled by geometric overlap rather than by temporal or camera-index distance alone, providing consistent extrapolation regime across datasets and methods. Evaluation without input poses. For pose-free methods, we estimate scene-level similarity transformation between the predicted source-camera poses and their ground-truth counterparts, and apply this transformation to the predicted Gaussian representation. The aligned Gaussians are then rendered from the ground-truth target-camera poses, and the resulting images are evaluated against the corresponding target views. Ground-truth source poses are used only for this post-hoc alignment and are not provided to the model during inference. This allows pose-free and pose-conditioned methods to be evaluated on identical target viewpoints in the same ground-truth coordinate system. A.

(17) (18) Opacity is activated using the sigmoid function, constraining them to [0, 1]. The spherical harmonic coefficients are used directly without an additional nonlinear activation. Coordinate alignment. During training, the predicted Gaussians are rendered using the groundtruth target camera poses for supervision. However, the camera trajectory and depth predicted by the geometry model generally have an arbitrary global scale relative to the ground-truth trajectory. Directly combining the predicted depth with the ground-truth poses would therefore lead to inconsistent geometry and camera scales, resulting in misaligned rendering supervision. To resolve this scale ambiguity, we estimate scene-level alignment factor from the predicted and ground-truth source-camera trajectories. Specifically, we compute the ratio between corresponding pairwise camera baselines and use their median as robust global scale factor. The predicted depth maps are then rescaled by this factor and back-projected using the ground-truth source-camera poses to construct Gaussian centers in the ground-truth coordinate system. The resulting Gaussians can therefore be rendered directly using the ground-truth target-camera poses for supervision. This alignment is applied to both the pose-free and pose-conditioned variants, since the predicted camera trajectory can exhibit global scale discrepancy with respect to the ground truth in either setting. Voxel Merge Strategy. GSNorm canonicalizes the representative single-view point spacing across scenes and camera configurations, but it does not by itself eliminate the variation in primitive density caused by multi-view accumulation. Since each valid pixel predicts Gaussian primitive, increasing the number of input views over the same spatial region can introduce multiple Gaussians at nearby 3D locations, making the resulting primitive density dependent on the number of overlapping observations. To reduce such redundancy, we apply spatial voxel merging strategy following AnySplat (Jiang et al., 2025). Specifically, we predict per-pixel weight map wp = {wp i=1 and merge redundant per-view Gaussians within local voxels. This produces the final unified 3D Gaussian scene representation G. GSNorm and voxel merging therefore address two complementary sources of scale variation: GSNorm provides consistent characteristic sampling scale for Gaussian prediction across scenes, whereas voxel merging regularizes the accumulation of primitives caused by overlapping multi-view observations. A.8 ADDITIONAL ABLATION STUDIES Normalization Space for Gaussian Prediction. The effect of Gaussian Spacing Normalization is evaluated in the main paper. Here, we provide more comprehensive comparison of different normalization spaces, including Radial Distance Normalization (RDNorm), Camera Distance Normalization (CDNorm), Depth Normalization (DNorm), and our proposed Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm). RDNorm is described in the main paper. CDNorm uses the median distance from all camera centers to reference camera as the scene-level normalization factor, whereas DNorm uses the median depth over all frames. Quantitative results are reported in Table 12. CDNorm is highly sensitive to camera trajectory: small camera baseline yields small normalization factor and excessively large Gaussian spacing in the normalized space, whereas larger camera displacement induces stronger rescaling. DNorm is less sensitive to camera motion, but normalizes only by scene depth and therefore ignores the pixel-space focal length and image sampling that directly affect Gaussian spacing. Consequently, changes in field of view or image resolution can still induce substantial variation in Gaussian-scale targets. To further illustrate the failure modes of CDNorm and DNorm, we examine challenging scene with small camera baseline and wide field of view ( 100). As shown in Fig. 10, both methods produce excessively large Gaussian spacing, but for different reasons: CDNorm is dominated by the small camera displacement, whereas DNorm fails to account for the spacing increase induced by the wide field of view. This shifts the Gaussian-spacing distribution away from that seen during training, causing the predicted Gaussian scales to be too small for adequate surface coverage and resulting in severe holes. In contrast, GSNorm canonicalizes robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing, providing more consistent spatial reference across varying camera trajectories and intrinsics. Training Design Choices. We further ablate four design choices: fine-tuning the pretrained geometry backbone, fixing the Gaussian centers, scaling the training data, and adopting diverse viewsampling strategies. Results are reported in Table 13. All variants follow the same training settings. The upstream WorldMirror 2.0 geometry estimator remains frozen in all experiments. For w/o Fine-tuning Gaussian Backbone, the Gaussian Backbone is also frozen at its WorldMirror 2.0 initialization, and only GSHead is optimized. For w/o Fixed Gaussian Centers, GSHead additionally predicts per-pixel 3D center offset, instead of fixing the centers to the unprojected geometry. For w/o Data Scaling, we train on Hypersim, while keeping the number of training iterations unchanged. For w/o View Sampling Strategy, we randomly select views and then partition them into source views and target views, while retaining the same numbers of source and target views. We find that fixing Gaussian centers produces the largest and most consistent gain across different inputview counts. When the centers are optimized only through rendering losses, the model can reduce image-space errors by moving primitives away from the geometry prior, resulting in geometric drift and poorer generalization to extrapolated viewpoints. Fine-tuning the Gaussian Backbone adapts the pretrained geometric features to appearance and Gaussian-attribute prediction, whereas scaling the training data improves cross-domain robustness. The mixed view-sampling strategy exposes the model to diverse camera motions and viewpoint changes, leading to more reliable reconstruction under sparse inputs and large extrapolation. 20 Figure 11: Qualitative comparisons across diverse scenes and viewpoints with multi-view input. A.9 APPLICATION TO PANORAMIC 3D CONTENT GENERATION. We explore SplatAnything for panoramic-image-based 3D content generation. We use WorldPano (Team et al., 2026) to generate panoramic image and convert it into cubemap perspective views with 95 100 FoV, which remains substantially wider than typical perspective inputs. These views are fed directly into SplatAnything for 3D Gaussian reconstruction. As shown in Fig. 13, SplatAnything produces high-quality novel-view synthesis under this challenging wide-FoV setting.
